deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three tables of discrete logarithms ('indices') for Gaussian prime moduli π, each of rational prime norm 𝔇 = N(π) ≡ 1 (mod 4). Each table has two parts.

(a) 'Potenzen der Primitiv-Wurzel'. Gauss lists g^k mod π for k = 0,…,(𝔇−1)/4. Each power is reduced to a residue of small norm by subtracting multiples of π.
- The table stops at the k where g^k ≡ i. Every other power then follows from g^(k+j(𝔇−1)/4) ≡ i^j g^k.
- The sign or associate of g is chosen so that g^((𝔇−1)/4) ≡ +i, not −i.

(b) 'Indices der Elementargrössen'. Gauss gives ind_g(q) mod (𝔇−1) for the units and small Gaussian primes q: i, 1±i, 1±2i, −3, −3±2i, 1±4i, 5±2i, 1±6i, 5±4i, −7, −7±2i, 5±6i, −3±8i, 5±8i.
- Apart from i and 1±i, these are the primary primes (≡ 1 mod 2+2i) taken in order of norm.
- To find an index, write q (up to subtraction of a multiple of π) as i^j·(table entry g^k). Then ind q = k + j(𝔇−1)/4.

Table 1. π = 5+8i, 𝔇 = 89, g = 1−i (i ≡ 55, g ≡ 35 mod 89).
- Sample reductions: g^5 = −4+4i ≡ 4−i (difference iπ); g^6 = 3−5i ≡ −5; g^9 = −6i ≡ 5+2i; … ; g^22 = −5−7i ≡ i.
- Indices: i 22; 1+i = i(1−i) gives 23; 1−i 1; 1+2i = i^3·g^18 gives 84; 1−2i = −g^10 gives 54; −3 = −g^7 gives 51; −3+2i = i·g^16 gives 38; −3−2i = i·g^13 gives 35; 1+4i = i·g^5 gives 27; 1−4i 15; 5+2i 9; 5−2i ≡ −g^8 gives 52; 1+6i 56; 1−6i 21; 5+4i 26; 5−4i 33; −7 83; −7+2i 63.
- The last column (−7−2i, 5±6i, −3±8i, 5−8i) was left without indices.

Table 2. π = −3+8i, 𝔇 = 73, g = 1+i (i ≡ 46, g ≡ 47 mod 73).
- Powers 0..18, ending with g^18 = 3−7i ≡ i.
- Indices: i 18, 1+i 1, 1−i 55, 1+2i 47, 1−2i 32, −3 6, −3+2i 8, −3−2i 45, 1+4i 23, 1−4i 52, 5+2i 66, 5−2i 35, 1+6i 13, 1−6i 3, 5+4i 69, 5−4i 31, −7 51, −7+2i 10, −7−2i 1, 5+6i 61, 5−6i 57, −3−8i 62.

Table 3. π = 5+6i, 𝔇 = 61, g = −1−i (i ≡ 50, g ≡ 10 mod 61).
- Powers 0..15, ending with g^15 = −5−5i ≡ i.
- Indices: i 15, 1+i 31, 1−i 16, 1+2i 35, 1−2i 39, −3 12, −3±2i 58/22, 1±4i 11/38, 5±2i 19/6, 1±6i 4/29, 5±4i 32/46, −7 53, −7±2i 55/56, 5−6i 1.

Purpose (my inference). Because g^((𝔇−1)/4) ≡ i, Euler's criterion gives the biquadratic character directly: [q/π]_4 ≡ q^((𝔇−1)/4) = i^(ind q). So ind q mod 4 is the quartic residue character of q modulo π. These tables are working material for Gauss's empirical study of biquadratic residues and biquadratic reciprocity for Gaussian primes (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, 1828/1832). They continue the series on the neighbouring folios (moduli 1+10i, 9+4i, −7+2i, 7, 5+4i).

Primitivity checks (mine). An element with g^((𝔇−1)/4) = i has order 4k for certain k. These are excluded case by case:
- For 89, g^8 = 3−3i ≠ 1.
- For 73, g^8 = −3+2i ≠ 1 and g^24 = −3i ≠ 1.
- For 61, g^4 = −4, g^12 = −3 and g^20 = 2−i, none equal to 1.
So all three roots are genuine primitive roots.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All 23+19+16 power entries and all 18+22+20 filled-in indices check out.
Incompleteness, not an error: in the 5+8i table the last column (−7−2i, +5+6i, +5−6i, −3+8i, −3−8i, +5−8i) has no indices entered.
In the 5+8i table the header 'Potenzen der Primitiv-Wurzel' is omitted, unlike the other tables.

results.what: Tables of primitive-root powers and indices (discrete logarithms) modulo the Gaussian primes 5+8i, −3+8i and 5+6i, for small primary primes and units.
results.modern_name: Index (discrete logarithm) tables in Z[i]/(π), i.e. Jacobi-style Canon Arithmeticus tables for Gaussian prime moduli
results.usually_credited_to: Index tables for rational primes: Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801) and Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus, 1839). Gaussian-integer moduli: Gauss's work on biquadratic residues (1820s–1830s).

results.what: Normalization of the primitive root so that g^((N−1)/4) ≡ +i. The quartic residue symbol then equals i^(ind q), giving biquadratic characters directly from the index mod 4.
results.modern_name: Quartic residue symbol via Euler's criterion in Z[i]; computing characters via discrete logarithms

results.what: Restriction of the 'Elementargrössen' to primary primes ≡ 1 mod (2+2i) plus the units i and 1±i.
results.modern_name: Primary Gaussian primes; supplementary laws for i and 1+i

deep.surprise_reason: These are correct, carefully normalized computational tables supporting Gauss's known research on biquadratic residues. Index tables for Gaussian prime moduli are exactly what one expects in his Nachlass for that work. There is no new theoretical content.
